Mr. Chairman, we can have little quarrel with the amendments proposed in this bill. They relate to the transfer of functions from the standards branch and from the Food and Drug Directorate to the department, and to the provision of inspection services. We favour these changes. We also welcome the minister's announcement that he intends to open regional offices. This would be a move toward decentralizing the administration. Nevertheless, it seems to me the minister has not made much of an attempt to outline the functions of his department in general.
I am not entirely satisfied that there was a thorough examination of this subject in committee. There were aspects of the subject that we had no chance to question at the time. Thus, while we are discussing the reorganization of government departments, I think we should take advantage of the opportunity to say some of the things which are on our minds. I want to talk for a while about the purpose of this department. As now constituted, the department has three branches-one might call them the three faces of Eve: consumer affairs, corporate affairs and combines investigation. Corporate affairs, the swinging, capitalist personality, is responsible for all matters involving corporations and corporate securities including such matters as bankruptcy, patents, copy rights and trademarks. In general, to use the words of the minister, this part of the department is concerned with administering many of the federal laws which regulate the businesses which supply goods and services. In this connection, the minister sees the role of the department as "increasing investor and shareholder confidence and enhancing the opportunities for raising capital." In addition he sees the department as an instrument for "ensuring probity in the marketplace." I prefer to take the minister's words rather than those of anybody else when they are available.
The combines investigation branch seems to me a most insecure and secretive personality. It is supposed to ensure a vigorous economy through a sound competition policy basic to a
Government Organization prosperous and vigorous economy. Again, I use the minister's words.
Finally, the consumer affairs branch is supposed to protect consumers from the abuses inherent in this same vigorous, competitive economy. I emphasize the word "inherent". It is supposed to protect them against fraud and deception by manufacturers through substandard packaging, inadequate labelling, misleading advertizing, games, gimicks and questionable credit practices.
In addition to concern about the safety and quality of products, the department is also supposed to be concerned with their price. After all, the department was set up after an investigation into the prices of consumer goods with particular reference to the price of food and the price of housing. I do not think we should lose sight of these circumstances. At the time, a great deal of credit was given to the boycotts by women consumers around this country as being instrumental in bringing that investigation about and giving final weight to the request for a department of consumer affairs.
The department was supposed to operate not only in terms of obscure and personal price indexes and figures relating to the performance of the economy but also in connection with the specific problems of people, including people living on low incomes, people living on fixed incomes and people without enough information to be "rational" consumers-people without proper protection.
The minister referred to the first aspect of these functions when he spoke during the budget debate on November 8, 1968. He said:
I rise to speak today because of my particular interest in the performance of the Canadian economy from the point of view of the consumer whom it is my statutory obligation to represent.
Despite these fine sentiments and some real effort on the part of the minister, the department has failed to deal with the most urgent problems faced by people. I think it is doomed to continue this failure unless at least two important changes are made. First, the department has to overcome its schizophrenic personality. Second it must relate directly to people, and learn to work with them directly.
As far as the schizophrenic personality of the department is concerned, the minister says it is his statutory obligation to represent the consumer. But because of the way in which the department is now constituted it is also his statutory obligation to represent

March 13, 1969
Government Organization businessmen, the producers. He himself recognized the contradiction inherent in this position when he spoke on December 9 and told us it was no secret that consumer interests and producer interests were often in conflict. Nevertheless, he continues to try to make these conflicting interests work in double harness. I do not think it can be done well within the same department. He said he was striving to obtain for all citizens just and fair economic treatment whether they were concerned with the supply side or on the consumer side of the market, whether they be consumers, investors or businessmen.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
The truth is that when they are talking to their business friends, the minister and his officials keep explaining away their responsibilities to consumers. I see the minister smiling but just let him wait. Let me again quote Gordon Osbaldeston, the deputy minister of consumer affairs, who by the way has had a long career in the public service looking after not the interests of consumers but the interests of the Canadian business community in the Department of Trade and Commerce. In my view this is not an ideal apprenticeship for looking after the interests of consumers. From a recent speech in which he said that free enterprise was the goal of the department, I quote:
We want businessmen to know what we are all about. That's why we start from the premise of free enterprise, and work from there.
This leads me to inquire: What is the purpose of the department? Is it to satisfy businessmen and the free enterprise system? Is it to protect the consumer? Or is it to give each one the idea that the department is on its side at one and the same time? Mr. Osbaldeston's view makes it clear that, in his opinion at least, the interests of business come first. And Mr. Osbaldeston is deputy minister of the consumer affairs branch, the official who is supposed to speak for the interests of consumers.
From the beginning the minister has insisted that, and again I use his own words:
A knowledgable customer is no threat to the honest businessman and certainly no threat to the market place.
Surely, it is not the qualities of customers that threaten the marketplace; rather it is the inherent qualities of uncontrolled free enterprise. The minister is keen on consumer education to deal with this, but education is a two-way process. It is not just a question of informing the consumers how to be more

careful shoppers; it is also a question of giving the consumers the chance to let the department know what they want and where they need protection.
The department has so far set up two new pieces of machinery that are supposed to carry out the function of protecting consumers. These are Box 99, the complaints department, and the consumer advisory council. But characteristically, the approach of both is impersonal.
As far as Box 99 is concerned, people can write to it if they know about it. Here, I give the department credit for taking steps to make it known. Possibly some time later on a letter will be received from the company that caused the particular problem, but what chance does one get personnally and publicly to discuss one's problem? Who knows about it? Does the department publicize the names of the companies that are taking unfair advantage of consumers? What measures are taken to protect other consumers from the same abuses by the same companies?
These are questions that I have had asked me by many correspondents who, as consumers, have had difficulties. The truth is, I believe, that the department of consumer affairs is not prepared to name names or even to provide an agency that will do so. It is simply too much interested in its heartfelt responsibilities to the business community to become effective in carrying out its over-riding responsibilities to consumers.
The second piece of machinery is the consumers advisory council, which according to its chairman ought not to look after shortterm, specific problems. Dr. Leighton has said:
It seems much less productive to me for the council to tackle highly topical questions, such as popsicles, than to study long-term problems.
Who, then, will study these tough, shortterm problems? Such specific problems- including popsicles-are the very problems that the consumer has to face day after day.
The consumers advisory council would, in my opinion, be well advised to hold its meetings not always in Ottawa but at various points across Canada, including at each meeting at least one session that is open to the public and at which consumers can make themselves heard. This would put real meaning into the term "participatory democracy". Failure to do this is to substitute verbiage for the real thing.
Another piece of machinery that the minister envisions is a prices and incomes commission. We, in this party, have recommended
March 13, 1969	COMMONS
and shall continue to recommend a prices and incomes review board which would be exposed to the full light of publicity. As the minister presently explains the function of the commission, this body too will undoubtedly engage in long-term, impersonal studies that will have little to do with the immediate problems of people. It, too, will be non-participatory as far as the consumer is concerned.
The proliferation of bureaucratic institutions which stand like a fence between the minister and consumers, coupled with the department's failure to give the public the chance to be heard, dooms the consumer branch to ineffectiveness. And this despite regional offices, which are all to the good and which I hope will knock down a few of the palings in the fence so that at least we can get the odd look at the minister and his department.
This fear of public exposure and review carries itself to the House of Commons. Why is there no standing committee of the house to review the estimates of the department? I address this question to the government house leader as well as to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. With all the other important departments having their standing committees, if the consumers of this country are also important why is there no standing committee of this house to review, in particular the estimates of the minister's department and to undertake special inquiries into consumer problems as they arise? I think this matter is very important and such a committee would at least permit some airing of these problems.
I realize the minister proposes that reports from the prices and incomes commission should be sent to a joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons. Why not send them to a committee that is directly responsible to the elected House of Commons?
In my opinion, business interests are already more than adequately represented in the other place. Let us not load such a committee with people who are not responsible in any way to the consumers. I think the House of Commons should have its own committee, instead of squeezing consumer affairs problems in with the already heavily taxed committee that considers the estimates of the department of health and welfare.

I intend to make just a few remarks. First, I want to thank the hon. member for St. John's East for his helpful contribution to this debate. As I explained to him this afternoon, I will be going to Winnipeg on Monday to meet with the Attorney General of the province of Saskatchewan, along with his counterparts from Manitoba and Alberta, in connection with the Batten report. This is a report of a royal commission appointed by and reporting to these three western provinces. Each provincial prairie premier directed one of his ministers to study recommendations of the Batten report and their possible implementation in their respective provinces.
The chairman of that committee is the Attorney General for Saskatchewan, Mr. Heald. I will be meeting with these provincial ministers to discuss the federal-provincial implications of the Batten report. When the Batten report was made public, it was immediately brought to the attention of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, now the Minister of Justice, who acted very quickly in having it referred to the combines investigation branch. At that time Judge Batten remarked on how very gratified she was by the fast action and speedy reaction she had received from the federal government.

Many of the recommendations in the Batten report have been made by other committees and commissions, including the one that Senator Croll and I headed. Within my department we are looking at a great many programs for the protection of the consumer, and in the course of time we will be dealing with many of the things with which the Batten report deals. Some have been dealt with already and we will be dealing with more which are general consumer programs. I should have more to say on this subject when I return from Winnipeg on Monday night.
With regard to the Alberts Royal Commission on Gasoline Marketing, I should say that this is still being researched by the combines investigations branch. It was received by that branch only a short while ago, but I did say in the house that it was not my intention to amend the Combines Investigation Act until such time as the Economic Council reports on the government's reference to it on competition policy.
I also pointed out that the Alberta royal commission appears to deal with many of the same subjects with which the 1962 Restrictive

I repeat it is not our intention to act on the Combines Act by way of revision until such time as I have the Economic Council's report, and I thought the Economic Council should have before it these various provincial reports.
I concur with the remarks made by the hon. member for St. John's East that we must avoid conflict with the provinces. This is essential, particularly in a new area such as consumer protection in which at both the federal level and the provincial level new departments are being formed and new programs being developed.
I think it is fair to say that in this area of consumer affairs and consumer protection, there is probably a higher level of goodwill and co-operation existing between the federal government and the provincial governments than in many other areas. We had a most successful, most useful and most co-operative conference of officials, federal and provincial, concerned with consumer affairs, last fall. At that time, it was agreed that there would be a federal-provincial conference of ministers concerned with consumer affairs, and the work leading towards that conference is going along well and apace. Therefore I, like the hon. member, am conscious of the necessity for federal-provincial co-operation. I think at the moment we have it. It is my determination to ensure we keep it.

maintopic: INCOME TAX-DEDUCTION FOR BABY SITTING SERVICE
INCOME TAX-DEDUCTION FOR BABY SITTING SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, two days ago I asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare this question:
In view of the news today that businessmen can now take their wives on trips and deduct the expense from income tax, will the minister now consider allowing mothers who work outside their homes to deduct the expense of paying babysitters?
For years some of us have been trying to get income tax deductions for several groups of Canadians. One group is workers who require tools and special equipment. These are people like mechanics, plumbers, carpenters and electricians. These people have no means of deducting these necessary expenses for income tax purposes. It is not permitted under the regulations. Another group is mothers who work outside the home and who, in order to protect their families while they are gone, must have babysitters to look after the family. These mothers, and there are thousands of them across the country, are not permitted to deduct these expenses for income tax purposes. This is a tremendously serious problem. I receive many many letters from constituents and others across Canada. I
March 13, 1969	COMMONS
should like to read one which I have from a constituent:
For the past 10 years I have been a member or the countless number of women in Canada's labour force who wholly support a family by working every day. During these 10 years I have provided an equally important source of employment to the individual who makes it possible for me to be employed by tending to the needs of my family while I'rn not there.
Now I pay this individual a good enough wage so that she is self-sufficient, even though unskilled, and has not become a burden to society.
However, when the end of the year rolls around and it's time to "square up" with the government I find that I'm not only liable for my own exorbitant income taxes but must also pay the tax on the wages I've provided for my babysitter.
This does not seem fair to me, nor does it seem fair to numerous women with whom I am in contact daily faced with the same situation.
As I say, this is one letter out of many letters I have received since I came here from desperate women across this country. In the face of the situation in respect of ordinary workmen and their tools and in respect of ordinary mothers working outside the home who are faced with the expense involved in having to have babysitters, we find a notice in the latest issue of the Canada Gazette to the effect that an employee will not have to pay income tax on money paid for his wife's travelling expenses provided she travels with him at the employer's request and that the main purpose of her going is to assist in attaining the business objectives of the trip.
A government official said the notice, which is not a new law but a new interpretation of an existing law, reflects a more liberal view of expenses advanced to travelling wives. Believe it or not that word "liberal" is not capitalized. It certainly is liberal, and I would hope that the party across from me does not accept it as a rule, because if ever there was anything that was an unfair interpretation and a discriminatory one, it is that. Last year the vice-president and general manager of the Toronto-Dominion Bank lost an appeal of the re-assessment of his 1963 taxes of $15,985. The Tax Appeal Board ruled that $241 which the bank paid toward the expenses incurred by his wife when she accompanied him on a trip to a bank meeting in Saskatchewan was taxable income. This is the case from which arose this new liberal interpretation of the Income Tax Act. The point I want to make is that in order to pay income tax in the amount of $15,985 this man must have been receiving an income of between $30,000 and $40,000. He appealed in respect of $241.
As a result of this appeal this broader interpretation was given. This poor mother to
DEBATES	6611
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion whom I referred, who had been out working in a self-respecting way and paying the wages of a babysitter, in all likelihood receives the average wage for women in industry. That average wage is around $2,500 a year. We have the government reviewing the income tax regulations which affect this man and others like him who receive incomes in the neighbourhood of $30,000 and $40,000. By implication, the government is saying it cannot possibly afford to allow the woman with an income of $2,500 a year an income tax deduction in respect of the money she spends on a babysitter in order to protect her home.
I want to suggest that this is discrimination of the most rank and unjust kind. It is an open invitation on the part of this government to businessmen to live high on the swindle sheet. The Carter Commission, when it reported on these matters, indicated that deductions made in respect of income tax at the time the report was made ought to be carefully hedged around and should not be allowed to get out of bounds. These deductions should be kept very carefully within limits at their existing level.
Now, the income tax regulations are being broadened to permit business executives to take their wives with them on business trips and to deduct their expenses for income tax purposes. There does not appear to be any hedging here. Who is to decide in respect of the purpose of the wife going along? Is there to be any affidavit to the effect that she is on a business trip? Indeed, is there to be any affidavit that it is his wife who is going? There have been cases where it was not. Is this regulation to apply to people all the way down the scale? Is it to apply to workers who are not presently allowed income tax deductions in respect of their tools? Is it to apply to their wives when they take them on business trips? This is an inequitable, unfair, unjust tax, and I wish to say so in no uncertain terms.

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
maintopic: FISHERIES-SEALS-REPORT ALLEGING FRAUDULENT FILM PRESENTATION OF KILLING METHODS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my grievance refers to the question that I directed to the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Davis) yesterday and the day before regarding a film which is once again being circulated around the western world and is

doing great harm to Canada's international reputation. I asked the minister if he would agree to having a memorandum, which very thoroughly goes into this subject, tabled in the house so that hon. members can read for themselves the real facts. Only today there was a demonstration at our consulate in New York City over the showing of this film on New York television a few days ago, and there have been demonstrations in Germany and other countries in western Europe. I am particularly concerned because I understand the film in question, produced by Artek Films Ltd., was commissioned by the French network of the C.B.C., Radio Canada. Reference was made to this in the Maclean's magazine edition of March 5, 1966. I would like to refer briefly to the memo, which reads as follows:
This has reference to your request for the facts we know concerning the first film made on sealing in the Gulf of St. Lawrence. The information we possess is given below:
1.	The film was made by Artek Films Ltd. of Montreal in March of 1964.
2.	The chief cameraman was Mr. Andre Fleury, assisted by Mr. Uwe Konemann.
3.	Mr. Serge Deyglun wrote the script and voiced it for the film. Mr. Henri Stadt arranged the background music.
4.	The filming commenced two days before the opening of the sealing season.
5. Before the film crew went to the ice, they allegedly asked for permission to do so from Fishery Officer Beauchesne. Mr. Beauchesne does not recall having given such permission to Fleury or Deyglun. but even if he had been asked he would not have been able to prevent them from going to the ice for the purpose of shooting film. The fact that seals were killed before the opening of the season, however, constituted an illegal act.
6.	Three, and possibly four Magdalen Islanders were employed and we have written statement from Mr. Gustav Poirier in which he states that he was asked by the people making the film to torment a seal with a knife.
7.	The film was shown on the Magdalen Islands on the evening of March 7th, 1966, at which time positive identification was made of three of the Magdalen Island hunters who appeared in the film.
8.	Following the showing of the film Messrs. Mark Ronayne and A. Arsenault and Fishery Officers Dudka and Beauchesne had a discussion with Messrs. Konemann and Stadt who were also present for the showing.
9.	Under questioning Konemann admitted that he had attempted to skin the live seal but that this had made him ill and one of the hunters shown in the film partly finished the job. He was asked for a written statement but said that he could not provide this since he was afraid of being boycotted in the film industry. He indicated, however, that if a formal inquiry was initiated, he would answer questions put to him.
10.	The hunter shown in the film using a rifle with a scope to shoot adult seals both on the ice and in the water was identified as Serge Deyglun. The killing of these seals was done out of season.
11.	One portion of the film had a scene with a Magdalen Islander poking at an adult seal with what appeared to be a knife.
March 13, 1969	COMMONS
12.	Messrs. Konemann and Stadt both stated that they did not have any control over the final version of the film; also that they did not lie the way the film had been done and regretted the impact it had on the sealing industry.
That memorandum to the Minister of Fisheries is dated Ottawa, February 29, 1968. Yesterday in a daily trade publication published in New York City, reference was made to the questions raised in the house by myself a few days ago. I will quote from that publication, which is called Women's Wear Daily, the retailer's daily newspaper. It refers to a New York official of the S.P.C.A. and reads in part as follows:
Thursday morning, he added-
He is talking about today.
-there will be pickets outside the Canadian Consulate and Tourist Office here. Placards with photos and statements will protest the Canadian seal hunt.
This film has been circulated every year since it was first produced under commission by Radio Canada in 1964. It has been shown extensively in West Germany and other western European countries, and in the United States. It has resulted in demonstrations at Canadian consulate offices and embassies in these countries. I suggest it has done great harm to Canada's good reputation abroad and is doing very serious damage to the sealing industry in this country, which is so important as a supplementary source of income to the islanders of the Magdalen Islands, the fishermen of Newfoundland and. the fishermen of Gaspe.
I submit that the very serious allegations and charges made in this memorandum which was submitted to the minister last year, referring to the film which is once again being circulated, are serious enough to warrant a parliamentary investigation. My purpose in bringing this matter to the attention of the house and the minister is to ask for such an investigation. I request that this matter be referred to either the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry or the Standing Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts for a thorough investigation. I ask for this investigation because the film has done more to hurt Canada's image abroad than anything else in the last 20 years. It has done serious damage to the Canadian sealing industry, and is doing so every day.
I know that the minister and the government are genuinely just as anxious as I and other hon. members to have this matter cleared up once and for all. I submit that the

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion only way this can be done is for the government to agree to having the matter referred to the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry or the Standing Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts for a full parliamentary investigation, so that Canada's good reputation can be protected.

My officials and I spend a great deal of time and effort trying to get the concept of box 99 across to people. Everywhere I go I speak on hot line programs. We send out mail, communiques and notices. My officials go on speaking tours and talk about box 99 all the time. We want to involve the people of Canada in that program, and this is the exact opposite of being impersonal or unrelated to people. This is one of the most people-related programs of the government of Canada. As the hon. member said, we do not go about naming people who have made complaints to box 99 and in this way getting headlines because the average citizen who writes to us with a complaint does not want his or her name in the newspaper. My officials are concerned with solving that complaint and not with getting headlines. If the complaint shows us that some criminal or other offence has been committed under the Weights and Measures Act or under an
fThe Acting Speaker (Mr. Bechard).]
agricultural products act, then we report the evidence to the appropriate authorities, either federal or provincial.
So, I do not agree with the criticism of that program made by the hon. member. I think it is one of the most people oriented programs of this government.
I will conclude by referring to the remarks made by the hon. member for Surrey and will mention only one of the three points he made, namely the one regarding automobile safety. subsubtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF A DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES AND FORESTRY, AND OTHER NEW DEPARTMENTS
speechtext:
I was interested in the remarks made by the minister about the proposed anti-combines legislation. This is my seventh year in the house and it is the seventh year that I have heard ministers explain why this month or this session is not the time to bring in legislation to do something about the spreading of the iniquitous combines which exist. We have had anti-combines legislation in this country for almost 50 years, legislation introduced by a Liberal government under the leadership of the long-time Liberal prime minister of this country, Mr. Mackenzie King. For many years, until the public realized the futility of that legislation, the Liberal party and Mr. King used to make out that this was one of the jewels in the kind of good, progressive government which they were giving this country. We have not heard much about that subject in recent years because there is not a person in Canada who does not realize that our anti-combines legislation is, to a large extent, futile, and where it is not futile, is a hoax.
The department has some very good people carrying out investigations into these combines when they have complaints. I can think of many such investigations, such as the one into the possible combine in the price of prescription drugs, investigations about paper, about paper boxes, and about glass. There have been dozens of investigations which were very carefully and capably conducted, as a result of which many combines have been found to exist and the cases were taken to court. Over the past 50 years we have had, I suppose, hundreds of companies investigated which I could take the time to name but which I will not because I am sure the minister knows the subject better than I do.
March 13, 1969

These companies were prosecuted and convicted not just once but, speaking from memory, as many as four times. The companies were fined and, until very recently, the maximum fine imposed on them was $10,000. Recently, the fine has gone up to $25,000. As the Leader of the Opposition said on other occasions, what is a fine like that? It is a darn cheap licence to steal from the public.
The minister said we had to wait for the report of the Economic Council of Canada before drafting amendments to the anti-combines legislation. I do not know whether or not the minister or the government gave the Economic Council a deadline by which they should report, but why do we have to wait for the report of the Economic Council? Is there any question that we have combines operating flagrantly and openly in this country? Surely, there is none if we study the number of successful prosecutions that we have had. Is there any question that the present legislation and the penalties prescribed by the law as well as the attitude of the judges have failed completely to stop combines and to stop companies from getting together in combines to set exorbitant prices? Almost from the first year I came here I have had on the order paper a private members bill, which has been discussed two or three times, in which I propose a simple amendment to the legislation, that an officer of a company convicted for the second time of being party to an illegal combine which milks the public should be subject to a mandatory jail sentence.
[DOT] (10:30 p.m.)
I am not one noted for feeling we ought to be tough on those who break the law, but I know that when I try to discuss this question I can hardly get hon. members opposite to listen. They think it is terrible I should make this suggestion. But I do not see why a person who robs a grocery store or a bank should go to prison while a corporation director, who may be a member of the Rideau Club across the street, should be considered to belong to one of the top drawers of society. I think he should be penalized in the same way. The government, of course, thinks this is nonsense. Canadians often tend to look down their noses at the way things are done in the United States. We tend to think Americans are not like ourselves, and in many ways they are not. Their legislation is not perfect but the other day they set us a good example, using legislation which is much better than our own. In the near future, the minister is to
Government Organization bring before us again a bill which hopefully will do something about reducing drug prices. I suppose we shall support that bill while pressing for certain amendments. But the minister knows, as I do, that this measure will do very little to improve the situation.
By contrast, look at what happened in the United States within the last month. Five or six of the biggest United States drug companies, all of which have Canadian subsidiaries, were charged in a United States court with having combined to keep the price of one particular drug, tetracyclin, at a price much higher than it ought to have been. Under United States law, after a company has been convicted of having been a party to an illegal combine, a consumer has the right to sue for damages. I am speaking from memory, but I believe I am correct when I say a consumer has the right to sue for triple damages. When the companies realized they were going to be convicted and that various state, municipal and other institutions such as hospitals, the veterans' administration and so on, intended to sue them in respect of the over charges they had made in the pricing of this one drug, they agreed to settlements out of court under which they would pay the sum of $120 million.
We beg, borrow and steal enough ideas from the United States. Why cannot the minister bring in legislation of this type? Why must we wait another six months or another year or another two years for the Economic Council to bring in a report? I have obviously more confidence in the minister's officials who have been working in the field of anti-combines legislation for many years, than the minister has himself. I do not think there is any need to wait for a report from the Economic Council. The Economic Council is a good group of economists, probably the best we have in Canada, but they can tell us only what we already know. They can document probably in more detail than is so far available the fact that in every important facet of Canadian life there are combines. I would point out that the Economic Council does not to my knowledge have lawyers on its staff, the kind of people who can tell us exactly what should be in the law if we really intend to do something about combines. These men are employed by the minister's department. The minister ought not to tell us tonight that he has to wait for the Economic Council to study this question.
There have been so many examples of conduct of the kind we ought to be suppressing.

Government Organization Not more than a year ago, because of the war in Viet Nam and because of the strike of copper workers in the United States, one major Canadian company which only a month or so earlier had announced the largest profit it had ever made in one year-I am speaking of Noranda

increased the price of its copper by eight cents a pound. I am speaking from memory. Why was this action taken? The answer is: because the market was there. And immediately, International Nickel, Cominco and all the other companies followed suit. I suggest to the minister that a combine was operating in this case. These companies got together and agreed they could get seven or eight cents a pound more.
The former minister of trade and commerce told us he would look into this situation. He did so, and then suggested we were very lucky, because in Britain the price had been raised by twice as much. But, Mr. Chairman, there was no need for this increase in the price of copper, an increase which led immediately to higher prices for all consumer goods in which copper was used. What did the government do about the increase? Nothing.
It is no service to the Canadian people for the minister to tell us tonight that he can do nothing about amending the anti-combines laws, laws which I think not even the hon. gentleman would defend as being adequate, until he has received a report from the Economic Council. After he gets such a report he will, I suppose, hopefully, tell his law officials to go ahead. That will take a year or two, by which time there may be another election and a new administration which will not even agree with what the present government might propose. I suggest the minister should tell us tonight that he intends to move forward in this field, and act not later, but now.

speechtext:
Because of the way in which responsibility is distributed within our caucus, I did not expect to have an opportunity to speak on this particular part of the bill. However, as a result of the arrangements made possible by the government, and I certainly wish to thank the people of the house in this connection, an opportunity has been afforded to me and I believe I should avail myself of it.
I have been interested in all aspects of Bill C-173 but particularly in the part which concerns the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. Everyone in the house expects a great deal from this department, more, perhaps, than from any other department with the possible exception of the Department of National Health and Welfare from which we also expect a great deal. These two departments, I suggest, affect the lives of individuals in Canada more than any other section of government, with the one exception of the department headed by the Minister of National Revenue, at a time that is shortly approaching.
[DOT] (10:40 p.m.)
I am pleased that authority over the combines investigation branch is remaining with the minister. I am sure that if the minister is able to make any immediate change in any of his new responsibilities, it will be here. In my office-I think the same is true of other members-I have row after row of reports made under the Combines Investigation Act dealing with such things as gasoline, tires, fencing, automobile accessories and so on. It has always interested me to note that after an investigation is completed, and due process of law has taken place, a company that has made $5 million or $6 million from a particular combine is only required to pay a penalty of, say, $10,000. The company is not required to pay back the money it illegally collected from the public.
It seems to me that if I were a bank robber any bank I robbed would want its money back. They would not think it sufficient that I pay the penalty of a bank robber, eight or ten years in jail, and that I keep the money I stole. The other day I read in a paper that somebody had stolen $1.4 million, I think it
March 13, 1969

was, and although the thief went to jail the court wanted the thief to pay the money back. Yet, we do not ask combines to refund their ill-gotten gains; payment of a penalty is sufficient. I am pleased the maximum penalty has been increased, but it is still not high enough to prevent the same firms committing the same offence again.
I can call to mind two combines as examples, flour and steel. In each case no refund was made to the consumers even though the companies concerned were found guilty of combining and illegal price setting. Although the court decides in most cases how much money has been made by a combine operation, it does not require repayment of that money to the people; although guilty of the offence, the combine keeps the money.
Why the distinction between such cases and bank robbers? If he pays his penalty to society, why cannot the bank robber keep his ill-gotten gain? I am sure that the Economic Council would not look at this question from the layman's point of view but from the economic point of view, how it has affected the industry concerned. If the industry is not particularly competitive then the penalty will be paid.
I am pleased to see corporate affairs retained in the department, because I feel it is here the minister will make the biggest impression. I think even the smallest effort will produce results in this field. Even though Canada is industrially developed it is not able to enforce the honesty of advertising as other countries do.
For example, a television advertisement shows a very attractive girl in a bathtub using a particular brand of soap. It is, of course, the best soap. The impression is created that if all women used that kind of soap, they would also be attractive. This is not true.

Well, I do not think it is true, but I would willingly refer the matter to the Economic Council for further study. It might even be decided to hold an investigation, and I would be happy to serve on the committee. But it is safe to say that most advertising of this kind does not guarantee the results indicated.
When I was a miner people would knock on my door and claim that if I bought, say, a blender I would save so much money on baby food and on other items that have to be predigested. I was told that if I bought a freezer
Government Organization I would again save money by buying under a freezer plan.
It always reminded me of a neighbour of mine who had a particular make of car. As people are prone to do, he kept telling me it travelled so many miles to the gallon and was the best vehicle on the road. We all like to think that because we do not want to admit we have made a mistake. I always used to laugh because the young boys would tell me that, having told me how far his car would go on a gallon of gas, he often had to stop the car and pump gas out of his tank because he was getting more mileage than he thought.
Obviously there is something wrong with the claims of people who knock on doors and tell the housewives they will save so much money by buying certain products. This policy just does not seem to work. I suggest that it is with this sort of thing that the m'nister of consumer affairs will have to concern himself.
If I may give another example, I recently stopped at a grocery store to buy an aerosol can. It seems these products have very little labelling to indicate the contents of the can. In some cases the can weighs one pound, in other cases 12 ounces and in still other cases eight ounces, yet the cans are all the same size. Naturally, it is difficult for housewives to determine how much liquid is in the can.
The same is true with other products. In this regard, I think the minister will find himself running into problems with packaging. For example, I have talked to many women who tell me that they really want the tea towel contained in a box of soap powder more than the soap powder itself. If the box were full it would contain a great deal of soap. Since it probably contains a towel, the size of the box bears little relation to the amount of soap it contains. The housewife does not know how much soap she is getting; nothing on the package tells her that accurately. Consequently, she cannot compare the prices of brands A, B and so on, of soap.
[DOT] (10:50 p.m.)
Another problem we run across is connected with the labelling of po sonous or semipoisonous substances. Many commodities, like aspirin, do not harm adults when taken internally in fairly large doses but can prove lethal to children. Many household cleaning substances are not marked "Poison" because it is not expected small children will use them. Many housewives of course keep these cleaning materials within reach of children
March 13, 1969

Government Organization and may not be aware of the danger to which they are exposing the children. The other day I read in the newspaper where a child swallowed an L.S.D. capsule, with disastrous results. An adult would have been affected differently. As for the child, its respiration stopped, heartbeat was reduced, and if medical attention had not been immediately available it would have died. Clearly, the child obtained a commodity which was not dangerous for adults but dangerous for children.
I also wish to raise the matter of grading clothes according to size. We seem to have no standards for grading the size of clothes. A woman may go to a store to buy a size 8 garment for a child, only to find it does not fit that child. Our clothing is made to fit average people; but since most children are either below or above their average in height or weight, clothes often do not fit. While sizing clothes this way may not be dishonest, it certainly is irksome to the housewife. These remarks also apply to shoes as well as to many types of wearing apparel for adults and children. The department ought to establish some standards with regard to sizing, so that we may know exactly the size of the clothes we buy.
Labels on clothes or curtains are often misleading. Materials that are said to be washable are found after washing to shrink. The same is true of dry cleaning. I have been to a local laundry and heard women complain that curtains which, according to the label, could be dry cleaned had shrunk after dry cleaning. Another complaint is that labels on some consumer goods are not specific enough to enable consumers to determine exactly what they are buying. Sometimes a consumer will not know if goods are being sold at bargain prices, mainly because labels describing those goods are not clear in their meaning.
Last year the agricultural committee visited western Canada. I had the opportunity of visiting several flour mills and was interested, on talking to grain commissioners, to find that flour shipped out of this country must be labelled accurately. We, in Canada, buy flour of two grades-general purpose flour and cake flour. Yet those countries buying our flour know whether they are buying No. 1 Northern, No. 3 Northern, No. 3 Milling and so on. Our flour is not graded in our grocery stores and it may be that the consumer is not buying those grades of flour to which he is entitled. The minister said that an investigation is being conducted into this matter, as 
well 'as into the matter of groceries in western Canada. Before introducing changes in this field, I know he must wait for that report.
Other investigations in other fields are being conducted in this country. In northern Ontario an investigation has been going on for a number of years into gasoline prices. No decision has yet been made and the price structure of gasoline in northern Ontario has not changed. The industry knows up there that it is being investigated, yet seems unconcerned. There would be no harm in making inquiries under the Combines Investigation Act public inquiries. People being investigated could make representations and we would know where they stood. A number of factors are involved in the matter of gasoline in northern Ontario. For one thing, there are too many gas stations for the area to support. That is the fault of the gas companies which have built more gas stations than are needed. Owners of these gas stations cannot make a decent living unless they charge exorbitant prices for gasoline, the result being that gasoline prices in Northern Ontario are considerably higher than in other parts of Canada. I point out that the blame does not lie with operators of the stations but with the big companies which have built too many stations, to the detriment of the community.

from companies who are defrauding and shortchanging the public in various ways? subsubtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF A DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES AND FORESTRY, AND OTHER NEW DEPARTMENTS

I regret the answer to all three questions is no. With regard to Box 99, my officials are and will deal with the individual complaint that has been made and make every possible effort to correct the situation. If there has been a breach of the law revealed by that complaint, we will take action to see that the person breaching the law is properly prosecuted. If the complaints demonstrate that people need education in a certain area, we will use our communique and other means to inform consumers of the possible dangers or hazards. If the complaints indicate that legislation should be passed, and we decide it should be passed, every possible effort will be made to pass it.
On the second point with regard to the consumer advisory council, this is an independent council and I am not in a position to decide whether they travel around. This council has a limited budget for the first year and for the moment that money could be better spent establishing themselves, hiring research assistants and getting some projects under way.
With regard to the third question, my concern at the moment is the establishment of the price and incomes committee and the parliamentary committee that goes along with that. That is my priority for the establishment of committees. As the hon. member knows, it is up to this house to establish committees. Last October and December, the committee on procedure studied the committees of the house and a consumer affairs committee was not established. The unanimous decision of an all party committee was that the committees of the house as listed in the order paper were to be the committees. They did not include one on consumer affairs.

speechtext:
I was somewhat surprised, Mr. Chairman, at the attitude the minister displayed toward my colleague from Van-couver-Kingsway, and the offhand attitude he displayed in this house this evening. I agree that his department is probably well versed in problems affecting consumer prices, but I cannot understand why the consumer must go to the department to get action. It is completely idiotic to expect people who buy a package of cereal to write to Box 99 to the effect that in less than three weeks an item such as "Shreddies" has gone up five cents while the price of grain has remained the same or has decreased. It does not seem proper in this modern day for the minister to expect people to go to his department for action.
There is a lot of talk about a price and wage review board. Prices and wages have gone up, but the government has done nothing to see why profits have gone up. If there is to be a price and wage review board, then the government must look into the question of profits. I am amazed a department will be set up under this reorganization without any recommendation from the minister to include responsibility for prices, wages and profits. If the minister would be serious for one moment, he would realize this has to be initiated from the top. It cannot be done from the bottom.
Letters have been received from senior citizens and families now subjected to consumer costs beyond their means. It is completely wrong that a department should suggest to these people that they must come to the government to find out why prices have risen. Any member of the minister's department could go into a store for one, two or three weeks and he would find out where the profits are and why the prices are so high.
It is strange the research people the minister mentioned cannot do something to find out why these prices have gone up. Possibly, it might be wise to go back a few years to the time price controls were lifted and see what happened then. Price increases followed immediately without waiting for wage increases. The price of steel jumped 12 per cent, but the government did not ascertain the reason for this. Transactions such as this are often put into effect in the stillness of the night without any previous announcement. The government did not do anything to stop excessive profit making by Canadian corporations from that time to the present, and no doubt will not do anything in the future. It is true that certain Canadian corporations were
6620	COMMONS
Government Organization prosecuted for price fixing, but at the same time as they were being prosecuted price fixing continued. The profits rose merrily without a word from the government or anyone else in a responsible position.
In 1966 the profits of Canadian corporations were $5.5 billion, all extracted from a population of 20 million people. I ask the minister whether this is fair. I would give the minister credit for initiating this program if there were somebody at the top who would take the initiative to do something about this problem.
In presiding over the trial of certain Canadian bakeries, Justice Boyd McBride stated:
It was a system of misrepresentation and fraud, a system of plunder comparable to meeting a man on the street and forcibly robbing him of his money ... practices of this kind perpetuated by so-called reputable companies must be scathingly denounced by this court and I do denounce them.
[DOT] (11:10 p.m.)
The minister knows it is many years since this happened. Since that time there has been no effort on the part of any government to do anything about the matter, even though a Supreme Court justice made such statements.
The Vancouver Sun of April 20, 1961, carried the statement of the manager of an electrical firm in which he admitted that knowledge of price fixing went all the way to the top and that he had been ordered to attend illegal meetings with competitors to stabilize the market. Hon. members left in this chamber, and not too many of those who voted to stay are here, know what is going on today. All they have to do is look at the prices of products on store shelves. I think it is shameful that the consumer is subjected to this type of treatment.
E. P. Taylor, who controls all but one of Canada's major breweries, has been reported as saying:
I am sure that we have the power to control prices and sales practices and while it may be necessary for us to start local price wars here and there to discipline a small competitor, I am sure the profits will prove most gratifying to the shareholders.
E. P. Taylor is recognized as a great Canadian, but I suggest that any Canadian who would make a statement such as that is not doing a service to the country or to those he is supposed to represent.
Adam Smith, a well known political economist, stated:
People of the same trade seldom meet, even for merriment or diversion, but the conversation ends in a conspiracy against the public or in some contrivance to raise prices.

DEBATES	March 13. 1969
Surely, the minister and the government must know that there is a conspiracy right now to raise prices. Prices are being raised, and the effect is greatest on those least able to afford them. We have now got to the stage where people have to write to a box number to tell the minister about increases, but this serves no useful purpose. I am sure the minister and his department look into situations that are referred to them, but after doing so do they really prosecute those responsible in the courts? Do they let the people of Canada know what they are dealing with? I do not think they do.
We must realize the defenders of the so-called tight money policy and of the profit system are those who are taking the actual dollars out of the individual's pockets. The government should be willing to tell these people that the country will stand so much and no more. A government big enough to stand up and do that would have the respect of the entire population. It would not be subject to the treatment that most politicians get, including the minister, when he goes out on to the hustings, finds large families in want and tells them to write to Box 99. I am sure he is not proud of having to do that in our present day society.
The greatest problem facing Canadian families today is the ever increasing cost of living. This is the first item mentioned by people in reply to questionnaires that I have sent out. Pensioners and others on low fixed income are going to lose their homes and everything else due to the rising cost of living. The results of a recent Gallup poll showed that 47 per cent of those questioned cited high living costs as the source of their biggest troubles. We can imagine the category in which the others are, when the cost of living does not bother them.
Since 1965 the cost of food has gone up 12 per cent, clothing 13 per cent, housing 11 per cen-t, transportation 10 per cent, health care 12 per cent and recreation 12 per cent. These figures are not up to date, but I am sure the minister has the most recent figures. In the same period, despite some unusually large wage gains in 1966-67, over-all wage increases have barely kept pace with price increases. Many hundreds of thousands of workers in low paid jobs have actually seen the purchasing power of their earnings diminish.
All members in this chamber, even with the great amount of money they are now receiving, know that the purchasing power of that money is steadily declining. We all
March 13, 1969

should know what it must be like for those with incomes below $3,000 a year.
Those who are hardest hit by spiralling living costs are pensioners and others on fixed incomes. They are our senior citizens and our retired civil servants. With this so-called inflation, those who were previously self-supporting can no longer be self-supporting. I suppose this is the type of people the minister suggests should write to box 99.
When these people are completely down and out, and have to go into nursing homes for which they cannot pay, they must go on the welfare rolls. We all know that at one time $4,000 a year was considered the minimum at which a person could have any reasonable type of living. This figure has skyrocketed since then. We know that there are millions of underprivileged people in this country right now, and still we sit in this house and piously say we are going to set up a Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. If the minister is really concerned with the poor people, then please let him do something. Let him initiate action and not wait for action to be initiated from some other source.
Some governments and some members of parliament suggest that labour is the villain responsible for all our problems, but this suggestion does not stand up to examination. If labour is not the villain, then it should be obvious that prices are being raised arbitrarily to increase company profits. I am sure we do not have to look very far to find what is going on.
If profits are a sacred cow to the minister, his department and the government, then that explains why the government does not act. More than anything else, the word "profits" is the root of the entire economic ills of the country. Now, Mr. Chairman, I should point out that no one in this party has ever said that an investor is not entitled to a fair return. It has been suggested that we would like to go after corporations and cut out their profits completely. This is completely false. Anybody making that suggestion is putting out a red herring. If this department were to have responsibility for the three areas of prices, wages and profits, then I would have more respect for it.
[DOT] (11:20 p.m.)
Many cases come to mind of individuals who have written to us and told us about conditions. I imagine every member of this house has been in this same position. We 29180-4191
Government Organization have the situat:on in the maritimes; we have seen the situation out west and everywhere else. I am sure similar conditions exist in all these areas. If one looks, I am sure one will find them, but if one chooses to hide his head and tell the people to write to box 99, he will not find these conditions. If we are not prepared to do something about this, then we will have to cont'nue with the profiteering racket we have in this country. We know that in a short period more than 200 Canadian corporations have been found guilty of price fixing, some of them two and three times. That is quite a record in respect of the corporations of this country. The average fine for price fixing in fact amounts to one tenth of one per cent of the firm's annual profit. Such fines are little more than a licence to steal. I am sure the minister is concerned about this, and therefore he will realize that if we are prepared to allow these robbers to steal the consumers blind we can sit here forever and a day discussing this bill.
I should like the minister to stand up and say he agrees there are three areas in so far as the consumers are concerned. I ask the minister to try to initiate some pricing examination in the supermarkets which we have today. If he or the officials of the department would do this, I am sure they would receive many more letters addressed to box 99. So long as the people themselves have to write individual letters, and do not know what happens in respect of convictions, we will accomplish very little.
In closing, may I say that I give the minister credit for trying to have a people-oriented program by means of box 99. I am sure it may be small consolation to him, after what I have said, that I mean what I say in this regard. If he himself will initiate an examination of this nature, I am sure the people will follow along. If the government is not prepared to lead the way in an examination of consumer prices, then the government can expect very little support from the people of this nation.

subsubtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF A DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES AND FORESTRY, AND OTHER NEW DEPARTMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not know whether it is the minister's misfortune to be in charge of this department at a time when everything is going up or whether, as some people might suggest, that since he is in charge of consumer affairs he is responsible for things going up. I would like to take the kinder view and assume he is just unfortunate that this happens to be an awkward time. I think the responsibility in respect of this type of thing is more than just doing
March 13, 1969

Government Organization something wrong; I think it is in not doing the right thing to change the situation. I believe this is where we might be critical of the minister. Since the problem is here, and since he has this department, I think it only reasonable to assume that he should have some responsibility to see that prices are maintained at a reasonable level. It would seem that often his job as minister of consumer affairs has only involved explaining why prices have gone up. I am not prepared to accept this. I believe he should be prepared to take some action to restrain prices and help the people meet the increased cost of living. I think he should get in motion.
I should like to mention a couple of items which I think are responsible for part of the increase in the cost of living. Not too long ago in the province of Saskatchewan, the Liberal government of that province instituted a prices commission headed by Mrs. Batten. She suggested that the stores there were overbuilt and that they actually outran the needs of the people. I would think that the minister perhaps would look into a situation like this and consider the recommendations made by Mrs. Batten. This might be part of the reason prices have gone up.
At the present time the Alberta legislature is looking into the problems of service station operators in that province. These operators are being squeezed. In this case, while the service station operator puts his effort into tne running of the station, the public does not benefit too much. It is oil companies which benefit. I wonder whether perhaps the minister would look into the problem of improper pressure being put on small individuals by large companies.
I suggest that part of our service economy is overcapitalized. I wonder whether there could be some encouragement given or some restraint offered in respect of some sections of our industry so that the needs of the public will not be abused. I do not think this is an ureasonable request.
We educate our people to a great degree so that they can go out, earn money and become princes of industry. One area which I believe we have neglected, however, is the area in respect of budgeting for families. I should like to see some education offered to housewives or family people in the field of budgeting and buying efficiency so that they would be better able to meet the changing conditions. I think this is one area at which the minister might well take a serious look.

There is one last matter I should like to mention. I had a letter from the owner of a bake shop in my riding. This gentleman produces a very good local product. He suggested that the problem in his case was different. He stated that the large bread companies were offering bread in this area at a rate with which he could not compete. If in the long term this situation should continue I believe there might be a reasonable argument that this is a service to the people. But what has happened in some cases in this type of thing is that the price cuts in respect of bread are maintained only so long as the small business remains in operation. Once this business has been eliminated, prices return to a more normal level. I think this is another area in which the department might become interested. I believe in efficiency. I would like to see prices cut in order to help those who have a problem because of the cost of living. But let me suggest there are many situations in this regard which are not desirable. I have referred this particular case to the minister, and I hope he will look into it seriously.
I am not too sure just to what degree it is necessary to have proof with regard to these situations. These things are a bit on the vague side. Is it necessary to show that somebody deliberately cut prices, that there was an actual combine, or is this little business just to go out of operation because some large company wants to see it go? This is a problem for the minister. I am not sure I have the solution, but I hope that he will take a serious look at it. It is in effect a restraint in trade.

Mr. Chairman, I shall not take up too much time on this bill, but I have been waiting for this section to come along so that I might say a few words about it. Of all the departments in government, this is one of the most important.

I think this is one facet of government where something could and should be done to control the sharp increases in living costs which are bedevilling the Canadian people, particularly those on fixed incomes. For quite a long period of time we have heard a great deal about the sharp increases in the cost of living. We have heard various political parties and individuals talk about solutions to these problems. Yet as time goes on we find that the problem, instead of getting better is actually getting worse.
March 13, 1969

I would like to indicate to hon. members my feelings about consumer price trends. Other hon. members have spoken about a number of aspects of this department, and I think this is one of the most important. It is a continuing fact. As time goes on, people realize that sharp increases are taking place in living costs, but from month to month I believe individuals do not actually realize the loss in the value of the dollar as far as purchasing power is concerned. A year can quite easily slip by without people generally realizing just how hard they have been hit.
From December, 1967, to December, 1968, the consumer price index in Canada rose by 4.1 per cent. In the preceding five-year period it advanced 17.7 per cent in total. This represents a drop of about 15.1 cents in the purchasing power of the consumer dollar since 1964. To put it a little more simply, a dollar today is worth about 84.9 cents in terms of a dollar's purchasing power just five years ago. I believe this fact should concern the House of Commons and the people of Canada.
Another very upsetting aspect of the consumer price trend is the fact that the 4.1 per cent increase in 1968 was the largest rate of increase in any year since 1951. We find that in a span of 18 years, 1968 had the largest increase in the consumer price index of this country. This means but one thing, namely, that this government has been unable to check the rapidly rising cost of living by the methods it is currently using. This is a clear indication that other methods should be employed.
I would like to put on the record a few more facts about the percentage increase in the consumer price index. To realize the seriousness of the problem one has only to go back to one of the most recent publications dealing with the period to the end of 1968. When one considers these figures you have the up-to-date facts. In the last five-year period, we find that the average increase was 3.3 per cent. As I mentioned a few moments ago, the increase in 1968 was 4.1 per cent.
Back in 1964 it started out at 1.9 per cent, and every year since 1964 there has been an escalating rise in the cost of living index. In 1964, it was 1.9 per cent; in 1965 the increase was 2.9 per cent; in 1966 it went up to 3.6 per cent; in 1967, it was 4 per cent; and in 1968, it was 4.1 per cent.
Members of the house are aware of the components that make up the cost of living index. I do not have to go into them all. There are some very general categories. We
Government Organization have food, housing, clothing, transportation, health and personal care, recreation and reading, tobacco and alcohol, and so on. Every one of these, almost without exception, shows the same steady climb. Some are, I think, a little more disturbing than others. We find that we talk in this house about regional disparities. When we look at the eastern side of Canada one thing that strikes me in these statistics is the fact that last year the greatest percentage increase in regional cities consumer price indices was to be found in St. John's where the figure was 4.8 per cent. This is an area which is. generally classed as one which needs assistance because of regional disparity. The city with the lowest increase is the city of Vancouver, where we find the increase last year amounted to some 3.1 per cent. This is an area where there are some substantial gains so far as labour unions and other groups are concerned. This is of interest. The areas that can least afford these sharp increases are the ones that seem to be hit the hardest.
Let us consider housing for a moment. We find that so far as housing is concerned, again the average for a three year period is 3.3 per cent, but in 1968 we find that it was 4.8 per cent, the biggest increase of any year over the past five years. We are desperately in need of housing units and yet we find that for those who wish to own their own homes the cost has risen by 8.1 per cent in 1968 alone and rents have risen by an average of 4.3 per cent. This is why members of the house are extremely concerned about these sharp increases. We ask the minister: What is he going to do about it? We are now at the start of a new year and when we look into the business sections of our newspapers we find that building costs have gone up and the cost of lumber has gone right out of sight. This will add to the over-all cost of construction.
[DOT] (11:40 p.m.)
Bill after bill regarding interest rates has gone through the house but the ceiling on interest rates has been taken off, and again they are rising. Every time a percentage point or a fraction of a percentage point is added to interest rates, up and up go housing costs. Unless some checks are put in effect by this house we shall find that 1969 is a worse year than 1968 has been as far as escalating costs are concerned. I do not need to say very much more; I have picked out two or three fields; they are all the same. But here is the question: who is caught in the squeeze? It is the Canadian people who are harmed most of
6624	COMMONS
Government Organization all, especially that large group of people who live on pensions, including those who retired years ago on an income which in terms of purchasing power at that time was adequate. Today, they find themselves in trouble.
This is the field in which action must be taken by the government. Surely, we can sit down collectively in the House of Commons and contrive measures which could halt the slow but steady erosion of the purchasing power of the dollar. Some of the necessary decisions will be unpopular, and it is quite obvious they will be out of line with present government thinking.
We have talked for years about establishing a prices review board. What is wrong with setting up a prices review board? Everyone knows there are a number of factors in this over-all picture. One of my hon. friends has just spoken about spiralling profits. These are a fact. I am convinced that a prices review board would go a long way toward keeping prices down. Price increases should be justified. What is wrong with setting up a board and telling any corporation: You must justify your proposals for price increases. Until this government and the members of this house are prepared to take steps such as those needed to constitute a prices review board I am convinced we shall see a steady increase in the cost of living, and the purchasing power of the dollar crumbling away. This will give rise to a host of other problems. The need to increase basic old age pensions is evident to everyone who can read. It is heartbreaking to see old age pensioners obliged to reduce their standard of living month by month while a bunch of politicians sit here in Ottawa afraid to tackle the basic problems facing this country. This is what worries me as a newcomer to this house.
I believe the minister is trying to do a good job and already some measure of success has been apparent in the operation of certain branches of the department. But if he really wishes to succeed he will have to be a pioneer in his party, and to be a pioneer in the Liberal party one does not have to be very radical. A great deal of ground has to be covered. I suggest the hon. gentleman should look into some of the ways and means by which the spiralling cost of living can be checked. If the minister does this he will make a name for himself in the Department. At the same time, he will earn the gratitude of consumers throughout the nation and do a real service to those on fixed incomes, people completely at the mercy of an inflation

that has apparently got out of hand and which to date has not been remedied by the government.

I would also ask the minister to consider another matter about which he spoke some time ago, though I have not heard about it recently. I refer to the involvement of young hockey players in contract negot'ations. If I remember rightly, when the minister was a private member he raised this important subject on several occasions, and I think it is a matter that bears investigation.
In northern Quebec and northern Ontario there are many local hockey clubs, particularly in relatively small communities, some of which are developing professional potential. But if these young players are put under contract at the age of 12, they may find themselves legally committed for the rest of their hockey career. I suggest this is wrong.
I am sure anybody interested in the development of hockey players will agree with what the minister said previously, namely that an investigation into this particular field would do much for the sport, particularly in areas like Noranda, Quebec, Kirkland Lake, Timmins and other communities in northern

Ontario. The minister has heard of many problems tonight. In this connection, I think we ought to ask the Economic Council to study the matter of advertising. Mr. Chairman, I welcome the inclusion of this clause in the bill. I wish to make one or two comments on it and I hope the minister will reply. I notice that, in the main, this clause reconstitutes the National Council of Welfare. It makes a few changes that perhaps are not too important or significant but they should be noted. Instead of the council consisting of the Deputy Minister of Welfare here in Ottawa, the deputy ministers of welfare in the provinces and a number of other people, the council is to consist of 21 members, none of whom is identified in the legislation. I will be glad to hear the minister's comment on this. I notice also that there is provision for members of the council to be paid remuneration and reasonable travelling expenses, something that did not obtain previously. But a couple of things that obtained in the former arrangement still hold. The one that bothers me most is that it is still provided that the National Council of Welfare may consider only those matters referred to it by the minister. In the wording of the legislation there has been a change from "Governor in Council" to "minister", which is not too significant. But the other point still stands, namely, that the council can consider only those matters that are referred to it by the minister. It seems to me, if this National Council of Welfare is to do a real job, give good, solid advice to the minister and be the means of our making progress in this field, that the people appointed to it should have
Government Organization the opportunity to put items on the agenda that they think are important and give their advice to the minister on those items. In my view this council ought to have prestige equal to that of the Economic Council of Canada and 1 hope the minister will agree to make some changes that will give this council more authority and more prestige than it has at present. I wanted to raise one or two other matters, but I see the minister is anxious to answer the questions I have put to him and I will be glad if he does so.

The reason for providing for pay is that by this means we shall obtain the services of people working in the social welfare area who otherwise, because of insufficient income, could not afford to come to Ottawa and assist us in this kind of work. That is why we have provided for remuneration. I think we are being a little more democratic by providing for this payment.

I have an amendment that would change clause 7c so that it would read "refer to the Council for its consideration or the Council considers appropriate."
